{{short description|Relates tangents of two angles of a triangle and the lengths of the opposing sides}}
[[File:Triangle with notations 2.svg|thumb|198px|right|Figure 1 – A triangle. The angles {{math|''α''}}, {{math|''β''}}, and {{math|''γ''}} are respectively opposite the sides {{math|''a''}}, {{math|''b''}}, and {{math|''c''}}.]]
{{Trigonometry}}
In [[trigonometry]], the '''law of tangents''' or '''tangent rule'''<ref>See [[Eli Maor]], ''Trigonometric Delights'', [[Princeton University Press]], 2002.</ref> is a statement about the relationship between the tangents of two angles of a [[triangle]] and the lengths of the opposing sides.

In Figure 1, {{math|''a''}}, {{math|''b''}}, and {{math|''c''}} are the lengths of the three sides of the triangle, and {{math|''α''}}, {{math|''β''}}, and {{math|''γ''}} are the angles ''opposite'' those three respective sides.  The law of [[trigonometric function|tangent]]s states that

:<math>
\frac{a-b}{a+b}
= \frac{\tan\tfrac12(\alpha-\beta)}
       {\tan\tfrac12(\alpha+\beta)}.
</math>

The law of tangents, although not as commonly known as the [[law of sines]] or the [[law of cosines]], is equivalent to the law of sines, and can be used in any case where two sides and the included angle, or two angles and a side, are known.

==Proof==
To prove the law of tangents one can start with the [[law of sines]]:

: <math>\frac{a}{\sin\alpha} = \frac{b}{\sin\beta} = d,</math>

where {{tmath|d}} is the [[diameter]] of the [[circumcircle]], so that {{tmath|1=a = d \sin\alpha}} and {{tmath|1=b = d \sin\beta}}.

It follows that

: <math>
\frac{a-b}{a+b}
= \frac{d \sin \alpha - d\sin\beta}
       {d \sin\alpha + d\sin\beta}
= \frac{\sin \alpha - \sin\beta}
       {\sin\alpha + \sin\beta}.
</math>

Using the [[List of trigonometric identities#Product-to-sum and sum-to-product identities|trigonometric identity]], the factor formula for sines specifically

: <math>
\sin\alpha \pm \sin\beta
= 2 \sin\tfrac12(\alpha \pm \beta) \, \cos\tfrac12( \alpha \mp \beta),
</math>

we get

:<math>\frac{a-b}{a+b}
= \frac{2\sin\tfrac12(\alpha-\beta) \, \cos\tfrac12(\alpha+\beta)}
       {2\sin\tfrac12(\alpha+\beta) \, \cos\tfrac12(\alpha-\beta)}
= \frac{\sin\tfrac12(\alpha-\beta)}
       {\cos\tfrac12(\alpha-\beta)} \Bigg/
  \frac{\sin\tfrac12(\alpha+\beta)}
       {\cos\tfrac12(\alpha+\beta)}
= \frac{\tan\tfrac12(\alpha-\beta)}
       {\tan\tfrac12(\alpha+\beta)}.
</math>

As an alternative to using the identity for the sum or difference of two sines, one may cite the trigonometric identity

: <math>
\tan \tfrac12 (\alpha \pm \beta)
= \frac{\sin\alpha \pm \sin\beta}
       {\cos\alpha + \cos\beta}
</math>

(see [[tangent half-angle formula]]).

==Application==

The law of tangents can be used to compute the angles of a triangle in which two sides {{math|''a''}} and {{math|''b''}} and the enclosed angle {{math|''γ''}} are given. 

From

:<math>
\tan\tfrac12(\alpha-\beta)
= \frac{a-b}{a+b} \tan\tfrac12(\alpha+\beta)
= \frac{a-b}{a+b} \cot\tfrac12\gamma
</math>
compute the angle difference {{math|''α'' − ''β'' {{=}} ''Δ''}}; use that to calculate {{math|''β'' {{=}} (180° − ''γ'' − ''Δ'')/2}} and then {{math|''α'' {{=}} ''β'' + ''Δ''}}.

Once an angle opposite a known side is computed, the remaining side {{math|''c''}} can be computed using the [[law of sines]].

In the time before electronic calculators were available, this method
was preferable to an application of  the [[law of cosines]] {{math|''c'' {{=}} {{sqrt|''a''{{sup|2}} + ''b''{{sup|2}} − 2''ab'' cos ''γ''}}}}, as this latter law necessitated an additional lookup in a [[logarithm table]], in order to compute the square root.  In modern times the law of tangents may have better [[numerical analysis|numerical]] properties than the law of cosines: If {{math|''γ''}} is small, and {{math|''a''}} and {{math|''b''}} are almost equal, then an application of the law of cosines leads to a subtraction of almost equal values, incurring [[catastrophic cancellation]].

== Spherical version ==

On a sphere of unit radius, the sides of the triangle are arcs of [[great circle]]s. Accordingly, their lengths can be expressed in radians or any other units of angular measure. Let {{math|''A''}}, {{math|''B''}}, {{math|''C''}} be the angles at the three vertices of the triangle and let  {{math|''a''}}, {{math|''b''}}, {{math|''c''}} be the respective lengths of the opposite sides. The spherical law of tangents says<ref>Daniel Zwillinger, ''CRC Standard Mathematical Tables and Formulae'', 32nd Edition, CRC Press, 2011, page 219.</ref>

: <math>
\frac{\tan\tfrac12(A-B)}{\tan\tfrac12(A+B)}
= \frac{\tan\tfrac12(a-b)}
       {\tan\tfrac12(a+b)}.
</math>

==History==
The law of tangents was discovered by the Persian mathematician [[Abu al-Wafa]] in the 10th century.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Katz |first=Victor J. |author-link=Victor J. Katz |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7rP2MAAACAAJ |title=A History of Mathematics: An Introduction |date=2017-03-21 |publisher=Pearson |isbn=978-0-13-468952-4 |pages=298 |language=en}}</ref>

[[Ibn Mu'adh al-Jayyani|Ibn Muʿādh al-Jayyānī]] also described the law of tangents for planar triangles in the 11th century.<ref name=Debarnot />

The law of tangents for spherical triangles was described in the 13th century by [[Mathematics in medieval Islam|Persian mathematician]] [[Nasir al-Din al-Tusi]] (1201–1274), who also presented the law of sines for plane triangles in his five-volume work ''Treatise on the Quadrilateral''.<ref name=Debarnot>

{{cite book |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cPGRYLlwbrEC&pg=PA182 |title=Encyclopedia of the history of Arabic science, Volume 2 |editor=Rushdī Rāshid, Régis Morelon |author=Marie-Thérèse Debarnot |chapter=Trigonometry |isbn=0-415-12411-5 |year=1996 |page=182 |publisher=Routledge}}

</ref><ref name= Bosworth>

{{cite book |title=History of Civilizations of Central Asia, Volume 4, Part 2 |editor=C. E. Bosworth, M.S.Asimov |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ELrRr0L8UOsC&pg=PA190 |chapter=Trigonometry |page=190 |author=Q. Mushtaq, JL Berggren |isbn=81-208-1596-3 |year=2002 |publisher=Motilal Banarsidass}}

</ref>

==Cyclic quadrilateral==
A generalization of the law of tangents holds for a [[cyclic quadrilateral]] <math>\square ABCD.</math> Denote the lengths of sides <math>|AB| = a,</math> <math>|BC| = b,</math> <math>|CD| = c,</math> and <math>|DA| = d</math> and angle measures <math>\angle{DAB} = \alpha,</math> <math>\angle{ABC} = \beta</math> .Then:<ref>{{citation|last=José García |first=Emmanuel Antonio |title=A Generalization of the Law of Tangents |journal=Mathematics Magazine |volume=97|number=3  |pages=274–275 |year=2024|doi=10.1080/0025570X.2024.2336633 }}</ref>

: <math>\begin{align}
\frac{(a - c)(b - d)}{(a + c)(b + d)}
= \frac
  {\tan\tfrac12(\alpha - \beta)}
  {\tan\tfrac12(\alpha + \beta)}.
\end{align}</math>

This formula reduces to the law of tangents for a triangle when <math>c=0</math>.
